After dog-fooding it for a few days the approach works overall, --batched-session N is usable now in practice, both with subagents and with parallel sessions.

But there is a failure mode, related to this logic (keep longest entry): 

You may have ds4 running for days, for various tasks. N is set high enough, so that KV cache slots are not overwritten due to concurrency in practice. 

Then, I work on something, and get a long conversation in KV cache. It occupies a slot. When new conversations / subagents start, they start with a smaller context. The current "main" conversation is now smaller than these old big conversations, so subagents push out your current main chat, not old, long finished conversations, which brings the problem back.

So, over time, KV cache accumulates a few long conversations, they're never evicted, and prefill trashing starts again.

Scenarios:

| Scenario | What "best" means |
|---|---|
| Single sequential session, any N | Baseline: every turn reuses its slot |
| Long-running server (days), sessions come and go, some finish | Finished conversations' checkpoints eventually reclaimed; no slow slot leak |
| Steady parallel sessions, count ≤ N | Each session keeps its slot; a new arrival evicts only when all N are resident |
| Main + subagent wave, wave width ≤ free slots | Subagents take empty/cheap slots, main untouched |
| Main + subagent wave, wave width > free slots (oversubscribed) | Someone must thrash — prefer churning short subagent slots over re-prefilling the long main |
| Multiple mains, each spawning subagents | All mains survive; subagents churn among themselves |
| Mostly-idle server, sporadic use, overnight gaps | Yesterday's *finished* convos evicted before yesterday's *continuable* main; a resumed session still reuses if its slot survived |

The solution which seems to work well for all these scenarios: add "last used" time to each slot. If the time since last use exceeds a threshold (e.g. 60min), consider the slot stale, and prefer picking it as a victim, regardless of its size.

Other approaches considered:

* simple TTL (worse, as with the proposed approach sessions over TTL can still reuse cache)
* pure LRU (worse, as it doesn't consider size, and can drop main session unnecessarily)
* some combined score for slots, which combines time and size (can work, but I don't like it, seems complex, and has unclear/hard to understand behavior which needs to be tuned)

This condition on GLM seems odd and AI found a counterexample:

```
A DeepSeek speculative block returns [CLOSE, EXTRA], where CLOSE completes a tool call and EXTRA is a subsequent token. Both have already been evaluated and committed to the session.

The server consumes CLOSE, detects the tool end, and stops with:
kept = 1
ntok = 2
stop_decode = true

In the final PR revision, stop_decode skips server_generation_rewind(), and the direct terminal rewind is GLM-only. DeepSeek therefore retains EXTRA, even though it was never consumed into the response.

For a successful Responses tool turn, finalization binds the tool-call ID to that longer session. A subsequent matching tool-result request copies the entire live history:

Expected: [prior history, CLOSE,        tool result]
Actual:   [prior history, CLOSE, EXTRA, tool result]

The response can finish quickly and the next request can report a cache hit, while still conditioning generation on the discarded EXTRA.
```
